findings.title: Background legacy writes use the request context and get cancelled when the request returns.
findings.body: Each goroutine builds its context with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)`, where `ctx` is the incoming request context. The handler returns right after starting the goroutine, and the API server then cancels the request context. The legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection usually fails with `context canceled` or never runs, so legacy storage silently falls out of sync. That defeats the "safe measure" the request describes. The same pattern is at lines 110, 135 and 163. Fix: start from `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, which keeps the request values but drops its cancellation, then add the 10s timeout.

findings.title: A failed storage Create is recorded as a legacy duration.
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. Unified-storage failures therefore show up in the legacy metric and are missing from the storage metric. Use `recordStorageDuration` here.

findings.title: A successful storage Delete records the object name as the metric's kind label.
findings.body: `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes `name` where every other call passes `options.Kind`. Successful deletes are then labelled under the wrong kind, and every distinct object name creates a new label value, so the metric's cardinality grows without bound. Pass `options.Kind`.

findings.title: A failed storage Update is recorded as a legacy duration.
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`, so storage failures are counted under the legacy metric. Use `recordStorageDuration`.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection timing is recorded as a storage duration.
findings.body: The goroutine runs `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` and then calls `d.recordStorageDuration`. Legacy timings and errors are mixed into the storage metric, and the legacy metric never sees delete-collection. Use `recordLegacyDuration`.

findings.title: Legacy write failures are no longer logged.
findings.body: The old code logged every legacy write error. The new goroutines (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) only pass `err != nil` to a duration metric and drop the error itself. When the async write to legacy fails, nothing records which object failed or why, so the drift cannot be diagnosed or repaired. Log the error inside each goroutine, e.g. `log.Error(err, "unable to create object in legacy storage")`.

findings.title: Legacy Update re-runs the original objInfo instead of writing the object storage produced.
findings.body: The old code wrapped `objInfo` in `updateWrapper` holding the object returned by storage, so legacy received the same result. Now legacy gets the raw `objInfo` and computes the update again against its own copy of the object. A preconditioned update whose resourceVersion or UID came from unified storage will conflict or fail in legacy, and a patch can produce a different result there, so the two stores diverge. `objInfo` is also used from a goroutine after the request has returned. Pass `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: res}` as before.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one.
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` stores the logger without the name, kind and method values. Every other method stores `log`. Use `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.
